action_criteria.expected_evidence: Glucose 88 mg/dL, sodium 139 mEq/L and calcium 9.2 mg/dL normal: no metabolic provocation.
action_criteria.label: Check glucose, sodium and calcium at this first convulsion to exclude a provoked seizure
action_criteria.rationale: A first convulsion warrants a check for hypoglycemia and electrolyte disturbance, and she blamed her earlier episodes on low blood sugar; nothing points to a provoked seizure, so the test is not essential.

action_criteria.label: Pregnancy test (beta-hCG)
action_criteria.rationale: A woman of childbearing age without contraception at her first convulsion needs a pregnancy test before an antiseizure medication is chosen: the result changes the drug choice and counselling.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal sinus rhythm, 74/min, with normal PR (142 ms), QRS (84 ms) and QTc (411 ms) intervals; no pre-excitation, Brugada pattern or conduction block.
action_criteria.label: Obtain a 12-lead ECG at this first convulsion to look for a cardiac mimic
action_criteria.rationale: A 12-lead ECG is appropriate at a first transient loss of consciousness, although the gustatory and epigastric aura, automatisms and postictal confusion already make syncope unlikely.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Left inferior temporal cortically based multicystic T2-hyperintense lesion, 14 x 11 x 10 mm, with a bright FLAIR rim, no edema or mass effect and inner table scalloping, most consistent with DNET (ganglioglioma not excluded); normal hippocampi.
action_criteria.label: Obtain a brain MRI with a dedicated epilepsy protocol
action_criteria.rationale: Ten months of stereotyped metallic taste and rising epigastric auras before a first convulsion point to a temporal focus; an epilepsy-protocol MRI is needed to find a structural cause such as a small cortical tumor that standard imaging can miss.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Left anterior temporal spike-and-wave complexes with phase reversal at F7, increasing in drowsiness, and left temporal TIRDA; no electrographic seizure.
action_criteria.label: Obtain a routine EEG with drowsiness or sleep
action_criteria.rationale: A routine EEG is the first EEG after a suspected focal seizure and can show a temporal focus concordant with the lesion; a normal result would not exclude epilepsy.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No interaction between levetiracetam or lamotrigine and loratadine that changes management.
action_criteria.label: Check interactions of the proposed first-line ASM with current medicines
action_criteria.rationale: Her only medicine is as-needed loratadine and she uses no hormonal contraception, so no current interaction changes the choice and the check adds little.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not dismiss the small cortically based left temporal lesion as incidental: it is concordant with the left temporal EEG focus.
Do not start an enzyme-inducing ASM (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin): it would make future hormonal contraception unreliable, and non-inducing first-line drugs are available.

Do not start valproate: it is not first-line for focal epilepsy, and in a woman who could become pregnant its teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risks restrict it to cases where nothing else works, within a pregnancy prevention programme.
Do not perform lumbar puncture in the absence of features of CNS infection or autoimmune encephalitis.

Do not start carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine without first testing HLA-B*15:02, given her South Asian ancestry (HLA-A*31:01, which predicts carbamazepine hypersensitivity in any ancestry, can be tested at the same time).
required_recommendations: Start lamotrigine or levetiracetam as first-line monotherapy for focal epilepsy, chosen because neither is enzyme-inducing, so future hormonal contraception stays reliable, and both carry the lowest malformation risks.
Discuss contraception and pregnancy plans before choosing the ASM; start folic acid.

Refer for multidisciplinary epilepsy-surgery evaluation aiming at complete (maximal safe) resection of the left inferior temporal lesion, which also gives the histological diagnosis; a standalone biopsy only if resection is unsafe or tissue would change management; presurgical evaluation including neuropsychology (verbal and nonverbal memory) and, where the planned resection makes it relevant, language lateralization (fMRI or Wada), since the lesion lies in the left temporal lobe, usually language-dominant in a right-handed woman; the memory, naming and language risks of resection are discussed with her as part of surgical planning.
Give laboratory and seizure safety advice: no working alone with hazardous chemicals, open flames or hot plates until seizures are controlled, showers rather than baths, and no swimming alone.
Advise no driving until the locally applicable seizure-free interval is met and explain the duty to inform the licensing authority.
Counsel on SUDEP risk and how seizure control reduces it.

avoided_actions.rationale: Afebrile, no meningism or immunosuppression and back to baseline: there is no indication for lumbar puncture.
No murmur, exertional event or cardiac history, a normal ECG and an epileptic semiology: echocardiography has no indication.
Gustatory and epigastric aura, automatisms and postictal confusion make syncope unlikely and the ECG is normal: ambulatory cardiac monitoring has no indication.

Back to baseline with a normal examination, no head injury (she slid from the chair) and no anticoagulation: emergency CT is not indicated, and the epilepsy-protocol MRI answers the structural question.
FDG-PET adds nothing to a first diagnosis with concordant MRI and EEG; it belongs to presurgical evaluation of drug-resistant epilepsy.

A standalone stereotactic biopsy of the left inferior temporal lesion adds procedural risk (hemorrhage, infection, deficit) without changing management: the concordant clinical, MRI and EEG findings define an epilepsy-associated lesion for surgical evaluation, and the histological diagnosis comes from the therapeutically indicated resection; a biopsy is reserved for a lesion that cannot be safely resected.

A standalone open biopsy of the left inferior temporal lesion adds procedural risk (hemorrhage, infection, deficit) without changing management: the concordant clinical, MRI and EEG findings define an epilepsy-associated lesion for surgical evaluation, and the histological diagnosis comes from the therapeutically indicated resection; a biopsy is reserved for a lesion that cannot be safely resected.

accepted: Focal epilepsy of left temporal lobe origin due to a left inferior temporal low-grade glioneuronal tumor (presumed DNET)

differential.key_features: Imaging cannot reliably separate ganglioglioma from DNET; the absent enhancement, multicystic cortical pattern and inner table scalloping favor DNET; histology decides.

differential.diagnosis: Focal cortical dysplasia (type IIIb, associated with low-grade tumor)
differential.key_features: FCD may accompany a DNET at the lesion margin (type IIIb); this is a histological diagnosis made at resection.
The small size and benign appearance could prompt dismissal, but the cortical location and the concordant left temporal EEG focus make it the epileptogenic substrate.
Excluded: hippocampi normal in volume (left 3.1, right 3.2 cm3), signal and internal architecture; the lesion is neocortical.
Suggested by the patient; no diabetes or glucose-lowering drug, glucose 88 mg/dL, and the episodes are stereotyped with impaired awareness and automatisms.

A stereotyped gustatory and epigastric aura, witnessed automatisms, a tongue bite, a concordant EEG focus and a structural lesion make PNES very unlikely as the explanation of these events; coexisting functional seizures cannot be excluded without capturing a habitual event, so video-EEG is indicated if the events change or persist despite treatment.

key_clinical_evidence: Six to eight stereotyped metallic taste and rising epigastric auras in ten months, two witnessed with impaired awareness and automatisms, are prior focal seizures, so the two-seizure criterion for epilepsy is met [ILAE_def_2014].
Left anterior temporal spike-and-wave discharges on EEG are concordant with the left inferior temporal cortical lesion with DNET features; its small size does not make it incidental.

Left-hand automatisms are usually ipsilateral to the onset but lateralize weakly on their own; localization rests on the concordant MRI and EEG, and the side of a tongue bite does not lateralize [Lateralization_2005].
Epilepsy-associated glioneuronal tumors have among the best seizure outcomes after resection, so surgical evaluation is appropriate at diagnosis [Blumcke_2017].
In a woman of childbearing potential without current contraception, a non-inducing first-line ASM (lamotrigine or levetiracetam) keeps future hormonal contraception reliable [NICE_NG217_2025].

patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Kapoor is a 24-year-old right-handed South Asian female graduate student in biochemistry who was brought to the emergency department by her roommate after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure that occurred in their shared apartment this morning. Her roommate reports that the patient was sitting at her desk reading when she suddenly stopped and stared blankly ahead. She did not respond when her name was called. Her left hand began picking repetitively at the sleeve of her sweater, and she appeared to make chewing motions with her mouth. After approximately 25 seconds of this unresponsive behavior, she slid off the chair to the floor and developed bilateral limb stiffening followed by rhythmic jerking of all four extremities lasting approximately 60 to 70 seconds. The roommate called emergency services. Paramedics found the patient confused and unable to follow commands. On arrival to the emergency department approximately 40 minutes after the event, she was drowsy but arousable and increasingly coherent.

On interview, the patient reports that immediately before losing awareness she experienced an unusual metallic taste that she cannot otherwise characterize, accompanied by a rising warmth that started in her abdomen and moved upward into her chest. She felt briefly detached from her surroundings before the episode ended her memory. She has no recollection of anything until she found herself on the floor with paramedics present.

She reports that she has experienced similar episodes of the metallic taste with the rising abdominal sensation approximately six to eight times over the past ten months. These events have lasted 20 to 45 seconds and resolved spontaneously, leaving her mildly confused and fatigued. On two occasions, her roommate told her she appeared to be staring and unresponsive, and once seemed to be chewing and fidgeting with her hands, though the patient has no memory of these observations. She dismissed all episodes as stress or hypoglycemia related to long study hours and did not seek medical attention. She denies any prior history of unprovoked seizures, febrile convulsions, head trauma, encephalitis, or meningitis. She has had no recent illness, fever, or significant sleep deprivation beyond her usual graduate student schedule. Her last menstrual period was three weeks ago. She is not on any hormonal contraception. She takes loratadine occasionally but has not used it this week.

neurological_exam.additional: Small healing laceration on the right lateral border of the tongue consistent with a recent seizure-related bite. No bruising or extremity injuries noted. Mild fatigue consistent with post-ictal state.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose accurate bilaterally without dysmetria or intention tremor. Heel-to-shin smooth bilaterally. Rapid alternating movements intact and symmetric.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light bilaterally (4 mm to 2 mm). Visual fields full to confrontation in all quadrants. Extraocular movements intact without nystagmus. Facial sensation intact to light touch and pinprick in V1, V2, and V3 distributions bilaterally. Facial movements symmetric at rest and with volitional activation. Hearing intact bilaterally to finger rub. Palate elevates symmetrically; uvula midline. Gag reflex present bilaterally. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. Tongue protrudes midline without atrophy or fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Gait normal with symmetric arm swing. Tandem gait intact. Romberg negative.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and fully oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Speech is fluent with normal rate and prosody. No word-finding difficulty or paraphasic errors. Naming, repetition, and comprehension intact. Registers 3/3 objects; recalls 3/3 at five minutes. Able to spell WORLD backwards correctly. Mild anxiety appropriate to hospitalization. Approximately 10 hours post-ictal at time of examination and has returned to baseline.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk and tone throughout all four extremities. Strength 5/5 in all major muscle groups tested bilaterally including deltoids, biceps, triceps, wrist extensors, finger abductors, iliopsoas, quadriceps, hamstrings, tibialis anterior, and gastrocnemius. No pronator drift. No tremor or involuntary movements.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Symmetric 2+ at biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar, and Achilles bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No clonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, temperature, vibration, and proprioception intact in all four extremities. No extinction to double simultaneous stimulation.
